newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European barge fleet suffers despite higher rates.
newsitem.headline: European barge fleet suffers despite higher rates.

text.p: Struggling European barge operators have welcomed steady rises in freight rates this year, but the improvements will not be enough to stave off major structural change in the industry, operators and analysts say.
Backwardation, when current prices are higher than those in the future, has forced oil companies to draw down stocks and transport products at greater speed and with shorter notice.
While oil tanking companies have suffered from the resulting lower stocks, barge operators have profited from the greater flexibility demanded by suppliers.
The bustle of trading during the recent Iraq crisis combined with low Rhine water levels to push freight rates to their highest levels since last December and well above peaks in February and March.

The prices were so high, at one point, that some product was moving to Switzerland from the Netherlands by train, operators said. In the past, barge operators say, freight rates have only risen sharply in winter when cold weather and a rush on products such as heating oil coincide.
Even outside the busy periods, prices this year have risen, resulting in a higher minimum freight price.
"Compared with last year, the lower end of freight rates has increased," said Dutch oil consultant Pieter Kulsen who monitors Rhine shipping rates.
However, the barge industry is still plagued by overcapacity, with about 1,600 barges plying between the Dutch and Belgian refineries and berths along the Rhine.

"The minimum prices are higher, but there are too many barges on the Rhine and throughout Germany. Prices today are just break-even. This is the fourth or fifth (consecutive) bad year," said Dick Heijstek of Otex, one of the largest barge charterers.

The problems originated at the beginning of the 1990s when healthy rates led to new entrants and fresh barge construction. Fierce bargaining by oil companies product suppliers forced the many barge operators to reduce their rates.
"For many of the players, the rates at the moment are just enough to cover the interest on their debts," said a charterer at market giants Van Ommeren.
The problems forced the European Union to extend its barge scrapping scheme for a further year in a Council directive issued this summer.
The "old-for-new" scheme, as it is known, states that for every tonne of new shipping constructed, one and a half tonnes of old shipping must be scrapped.

The European Union hopes the barge fleet will decline by five percent each year and thereby fall by a total of around 15 percent by the end of 1999. To encourage the move, the European Union injected 20 million Ecus for one year.
"The policy was endorsed in June of this year and should go some way to solving the problem of oversupply," said EU transport commission spokeswoman Sarah Lambert.
Charterers agree capacity must be cut, but are sceptical of long-term success as the EU withdraws its involvement in the push towards complete market liberalisation by January 2000.
"(A capacity reduction of) 10 to 15 percent should be enough.... but when the prices increase, we risk returning to the problem (of overcapacity) again," said Heijstek.
